title: Beyond The Beacon: State And Corporate Competition After An Information-Rich Technosignature Detection
excerpt: The 2026 update to the Declaration of Principles Concerning the Conduct of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence provides a framework for post-detection practice.
content:
[astro-ph.IM] The 2026 update to the Declaration of Principles Concerning the Conduct of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence provides a framework for post-detection practice.

Like earlier versions, it addresses information content directly: a confirmation report should record any detected content, and the underlying data, methods, and code should be openly preserved and disseminated.

The declaration is necessarily concise and is intended to be supported by supplementary material that examines specific issues in greater depth. This paper contributes to that process by considering the possible detection of an information-rich technosignature: a signal carrying data, imagery, or machine-readable content.

Whereas the prevailing concept of a detection remains that of a beacon, a signal with recoverable and potentially exploitable content would shift much of the post-detection challenge from verification to information stewardship, while encouraging competitive efforts to decode and use the signal.

Few studies have addressed this scenario directly, and the geopolitical literature has so far framed post-detection competition mainly in terms of state actors. Large corporations now possess the computing power, AI capabilities, and, in some cases, receiving infrastructure needed to independently pursue an extraterrestrial signal without any obligation to disclose their findings.

This largely unexamined dimension materially changes the post-detection landscape. These considerations bear directly on the declaration’s commitment to openness and transparency, and on how that commitment can be upheld when powerful actors outside the SETI community may not share it.

I identify information-rich technosignatures as a topic for supplementary guidance and offer a preliminary set of questions for the community to consider.

Michael Garrett
